content: The following are professional summaries of the referenced studies and findings: 1. Donegan KL et al. investigated the prevalence of mutations associated with darunavir resistance in children infected with HIV-1 in the UK. Their findings were published in Antiviral Therapy in 2012. 2. The PENPACT-1 Study Team compared first-line antiretroviral therapy using protease inhibitors versus non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors in HIV-infected children. They also evaluated the impact of switching therapy at high versus low viral loads. This open-label, randomized phase 2/3 trial was published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2011. 3. Fitzgerald F, Penazzato M, and Gibb D reviewed the development of antiretroviral resistance in children with HIV in lowand middle-income countries. Their work is in press in the Journal of Infectious Diseases. 4. Achan J et al. explored the use of antiretroviral agents for malaria prevention in HIV-infected Ugandan children. Their study was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2012. 5. Kuhn L et al. conducted a long-term follow-up of a randomized, open-label trial examining the effects of switching children previously exposed to nevirapine to a nevirapine-based regimen after initial suppression with a protease inhibitor-based regimen. The results were published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2012. 6. The NEVEREST 3 trial evaluated treatment options for children exposed to protease inhibitors. Details of the trial were accessed in May 2013. 7. The ARROW trial team conducted a five-year open-label randomized factorial trial comparing routine versus clinically driven laboratory monitoring and first-line antiretroviral therapy strategies in African children with HIV. The findings were published in The Lancet in 2013. 8. The Paediatric European Network for Treatment of AIDS (PENTA) compared dual nucleoside-analogue reverse transcriptase inhibitor regimens with and without nelfinavir in treatment-naïve children with HIV-1. The PENTA 5 randomized trial was published in The Lancet in 2002. 9. Pillay D et al. provided recommendations on the implications of HIV drug resistance for firstand second-line therapies in resource-limited settings. Their work is in press in Antiviral Therapy. 10. Tolle M et al. analyzed reverse transcriptase genotypes in pediatric patients failing initial antiretroviral therapy in Gaborone, Botswana. Their findings were published in the Journal of the International Association of Physicians in AIDS Care in 2012. 11. Hazra R et al. studied the use of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate with an optimized background regimen as salvage therapy for pediatric HIV infection. This study was published in Pediatrics in 2005. 12. Purdy J et al. reported decreased bone mineral density associated with off-label tenofovir use in HIV-infected children and adolescents. Their findings appeared in the Journal of Pediatrics in 2008. 13. Tang MW, Kanki PJ, and Shafer RW reviewed the virological efficacy of WHO-recommended tenofovir-containing regimens for initial HIV therapy. Their work was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2012. 14. van Dijk JH et al. evaluated the effectiveness of efavirenz-based regimens in young HIV-infected children treated for tuberculosis in resource-limited settings. Their study was published in PLoS One in 2013. 15. Meya D et al. assessed the cost-effectiveness of serum cryptococcal antigen screening to prevent deaths among HIV-infected individuals with CD4+ counts below 100 cells/μL starting therapy in resource-limited settings. Their findings were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2010. 16. Loutfy MR et al. conducted a systematic review of HIV transmission between heterosexual serodiscordant couples where the HIV-positive partner was fully suppressed on antiretroviral therapy. The study was published in PLoS One in 2013. 17. Rutherford GW et al. systematically reviewed the performance of the 2010 WHO immunologic and clinical criteria for predicting virologic failure in patients on antiretroviral therapy. This was presented at the 7th IAS Conference on HIV Pathogenesis, Treatment, and Prevention in 2013. 18. Orrell C et al. examined the conservation of first-line antiretroviral treatment regimens in settings with limited therapeutic options. Their findings were published in Antiviral Therapy in 2007. 19. Mermin J et al. evaluated the utility of routine viral load, CD4 cell count, and clinical monitoring among adults with HIV receiving antiretroviral therapy in Uganda. This randomized trial was published in BMJ in 2011. 20. Jourdain G et al. conducted the PHPT-3 randomized clinical trial comparing CD4 versus viral load monitoring and switching strategies in Thailand. Details were accessed in May 2013. 21. Saag MS et al. performed a cluster-randomized trial of routine versus discretionary viral load monitoring among adults starting ART in Zambia. This was presented at the 19th Annual Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections. 22. Keiser O et al. assessed the accuracy of WHO CD4 cell count criteria for virological failure of antiretroviral therapy. Their findings were published in Tropical Medicine and International Health in 2009. 23. Abouyannis M et al. developed and validated systems for rational use of viral load testing in adults receiving first-line ART in sub-Saharan Africa. Their study was published in AIDS in 2011. 24. Chaiwarith R et al. Their findings were published in the International Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2007. 25. Hosseinipour M et al. validated clinical and immunological definitions of ART failure in Malawi. Details were accessed in May 2013. 26. Kantor R et al. highlighted the misclassification of first-line ART failure based on immunological monitoring in resource-limited settings. Their study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2009. 27. Labhardt ND et al. developed a clinical prediction score in addition to WHO criteria for ART failure in resource-limited settings, based on experience from Lesotho. Their findings were published in PLoS One in 2012. 28. Mee P et al. evaluated WHO criteria for ART failure in adults in South Africa. Their study was published in AIDS in 2008. 29. Moore DM et al. demonstrated that CD4+ T-cell count monitoring does not accurately identify virologic failure in HIV-infected adults receiving ART. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2008. 30. Rawizza H et al. found that immunologic criteria are poor predictors of virologic outcomes, with implications for HIV treatment monitoring in resource-limited settings. Their study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2011. 31. Rewari BB evaluated the role of targeted viral load testing in assessing patients for second-line ART in India. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2010. 32. Reynolds SJ et al. reported the failure of immunologic criteria to appropriately identify ART failure in Uganda. Their study was published in AIDS in 2009. 33. van Oosterhout JJ et al. assessed the diagnosis of ART failure in Malawi, finding poor performance of clinical and immunological WHO criteria. Their findings were published in Tropical Medicine and International Health in 2009. 34. Barlow-Mosha L et al. validated WHO 2010 immunologic criteria for predicting pediatric first-line ART failure in Uganda, concluding that CD4 is a poor surrogate for virologic monitoring. Details were accessed in May 2013. 35. Davies MA et al. evaluated the accuracy of immunologic criteria for identifying virologic failure in children on ART in the IeDEA Southern Africa Collaboration. Their findings were published in Tropical Medicine and International Health in 2011. 36. Davies MA et al. explored the role of targeted viral load testing in diagnosing virologic failure in children on ART with immunologic failure. Their findings are in press. 37. Westley BP et al. found that the 2010 WHO guidelines for predicting treatment failures in Cambodian children were associated with high misclassification rates and drug resistance. Their study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2012. 38. Laurent C et al. compared monitoring strategies for ART in rural Cameroon, finding that clinical monitoring alone was non-inferior to laboratory-based monitoring. Their findings were published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2011. 39. Mugyenyi P et al. conducted the DART trial, comparing routine versus clinically driven laboratory monitoring of ART in Africa. Their findings were published in The Lancet in 2010. 40. Havlir DV et al. examined the prevalence and predictive value of intermittent viremia with combination HIV therapy. Their study was published in JAMA in 2001. 41. Mocroft A et al. assessed the safety of discontinuing primary Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia prophylaxis in virologically suppressed HIV patients with CD4 counts below 200 cells/μL. Their findings were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2010. 42. Gale HB et al. questioned the necessity of frequent CD4+ T-lymphocyte count monitoring in patients with counts ≥300 cells/μL and HIV-1 suppression. Their findings are in press. 43. Johannessen A et al. demonstrated the effectiveness of dried blood spots for viral load monitoring in patients receiving ART in rural Tanzania. Their study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2009. 44. Garrido C et al. Their findings were published in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology in 2009. 45. Monleau M et al. evaluated RNA extraction methods and storage conditions for dried plasma or blood spots for HIV-1 RNA quantification and drug resistance testing. Their study was published in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology in 2009. 46. Steinmetzer K et al. explored HIV load testing using small samples of whole blood. Their findings were published in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology in 2010. 47. Viljoen J et al. quantified HIV-1 RNA using dried blood spots in South Africa and Burkina Faso. Their study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2010. 48. Bonjoch A et al. reported a high rate of reversibility of renal damage in HIV-infected patients receiving tenofovir-containing ART. Their findings were published in Antiviral Research in 2012. 49. Treatment guidelines for tuberculosis and malaria were accessed in May 2013. 50. Johnson M et al. compared the efficacy and safety of once-daily atazanavir/ritonavir versus twice-daily lopinavir/ritonavir in patients with multiple virologic failures. Their findings were published in AIDS in 2006. 51. Arasteh K et al. evaluated the efficacy and safety of darunavir/ritonavir in treatment-experienced HIV-1 patients in the POWER trials. Their findings were published in Antiviral Therapy in 2009. 52. Banhegyi D et al. compared darunavir/ritonavir versus lopinavir/ritonavir in treatment-experienced patients in the TITAN study. Their findings were published in Current HIV Research in 2012. 53. Molina JM et al. compared once-daily atazanavir/ritonavir with twice-daily lopinavir/ritonavir in ART-naïve HIV-1 patients in the CASTLE study. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2010. 54. Josephson F et al. Their findings were published in the European Journal of Clinical Pharmacology in 2010. 55. Orkin C et al. reported the final 192-week efficacy and safety of once-daily darunavir/ritonavir versus lopinavir/ritonavir in the ARTEMIS trial. Their findings are in press. 56. Acosta EP et al. studied the pharmacokinetics and safety of atazanavir administered with rifampin. Their findings were published in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy in 2007. 57. Burger DM et al. evaluated the pharmacokinetics of atazanavir/ritonavir with rifampin in healthy volunteers. Their findings were published in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy in 2006. 58. Justesen US et al. investigated the pharmacokinetic interaction between rifampin and indinavir/ritonavir in HIV-infected patients. Their findings were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2004. 59. LaPorte C et al. studied the pharmacokinetics of adjusted-dose lopinavir/ritonavir with rifampin in healthy volunteers. Their findings were published in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy in 2004. 60. Decloedt EH et al. evaluated the pharmacokinetics of lopinavir in HIV-infected adults receiving rifampin with adjusted doses of lopinavir/ritonavir tablets. Their findings were published in Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy in 2011. 61. Taylor BS et al. reported the rapid development of antiretroviral drug resistance mutations in HIV-infected children under two years of age initiating protease inhibitor-based therapy in South Africa. Their findings were published in AIDS Research and Human Retroviruses in 2011. 62. Zanoni B et al. identified predictors of poor CD4 and weight recovery in HIV-infected children initiating ART in South Africa. Their findings were published in PLoS One in 2012. 63. Orrell C et al. examined resistance in pediatric patients experiencing virologic failure with firstand second-line ART. Their findings are in press. 64. van Zyl GU et al. reported protease inhibitor resistance in South African children with virologic failure. Their findings were published in the Pediatric Infectious Diseases Journal in 2009. 65. King JR et al. reviewed antiretroviral pharmacokinetics in the pediatric population. Their findings were published in Clinical Pharmacokinetics in 2002. 66. The KONCERT trial evaluated the pharmacokinetics, safety, and efficacy of once-daily versus twice-daily lopinavir/ritonavir tablets in HIV-1-infected children. Details were accessed in May 2013. 67. Bakeera-Kitaka S et al. studied the pharmacokinetics and acceptability of a new generic lopinavir/ritonavir sprinkle formulation in African HIV-positive children aged 1–4 years. Details were accessed in May 2013. 68. Gotte M et al. demonstrated that the M184V mutation in HIV-1 reverse transcriptase impairs the rescue of chain-terminated DNA synthesis. Their findings were published in the Journal of Virology in 2000. 69. Ajose O et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of treatment outcomes for patients on second-line ART in resource-limited settings. Their findings were published in AIDS in 2012. 70. Gatell JM et al. reported the long-term efficacy and safety of the HIV integrase inhibitor raltegravir in patients with limited treatment options in a Phase II study. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2010. 71. Steigbigel RT et al. evaluated the long-term efficacy and safety of raltegravir combined with optimized background therapy in treatment-experienced patients with drug-resistant HIV infection. Their findings were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2010. 72. Katlama C et al. assessed the efficacy and safety of etravirine at week 96 in treatment-experienced HIV-1-infected patients in the DUET-1 and DUET-2 trials. Their findings were published in Antiviral Therapy in 2010. 73. Imaz A et al. evaluated the efficacy and safety of nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor-sparing salvage therapy for multidrug-resistant HIV-1 infection. Their findings were published in the Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy in 2011. 74. Fagard C et al. reported the long-term efficacy and safety of raltegravir, etravirine, and darunavir/ritonavir in treatment-experienced patients in the ANRS 139 TRIO trial. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2012.
